title: Akiva and the Water on the Stone
text:
According to the tradition preserved in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Akiva had reached the age of forty without learning anything. He was an unlettered man, and it seemed far too late for him to begin the study of the Torah, which scholars spent their whole lives mastering.

One day he was standing by a well and noticed a stone at its mouth with a deep hollow worn into it. He asked who had carved it. He was told that it was the water, which fell on it constantly, drop by drop, day after day.

Akiva thought about this. If something as soft as water could carve its way into something as hard as stone, how much more could the words of the Torah, which are as hard as iron, carve their way into his heart, which was only flesh and blood.

He went straight off to study. With his young son, he sat with the children at a teacher's side and began with the alphabet, writing the letters on a tablet. He went on, letter by letter and teaching by teaching, until he had learned the whole Torah. Rabbi Akiva became one of the greatest scholars in Jewish history.
lesson: It is rarely too late to start. Small efforts repeated every day can wear through what looks impossibly hard.
source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Version A, Chapter 6
caveat: This account of Akiva's beginnings is a traditional story from rabbinic literature compiled centuries after his death.
